heading: Three arrivals, one surname
lead: This archive is named for a surname, and the surname is the least reliable thing in it. Three separate families of it reached this coast within fifty years of each other, out of three different places, for three different reasons, and only one of them is the family this site descends from. They have been confused with one another for two centuries — in print, in nobiliary compilations, and most recently in an online tree copied outward since 2017. What follows is the distinction stated once, plainly.

cards.text: Venetian colonists in Crete. Nicolò de Franceschi was castellan of Castel Milopotamo in 1500, and his son **Luca di Nicolò** is the first of the name actually proved in the nobiliary registers of the Archive of the Duke of Candia. In the Veneto-Turkish war they held the Cretan ports of Colus, Lemiores and Sabbionera with the vassals of their county, at their own expense. On 30 December 1669 **Marcantonio Querini, Duke of Candia**, confirmed them in *mero et mixto imperio*; Zaccaria Mocenigo renewed the comital title in 1688. Then Candia fell. Morosini's galleys took off the Venetian families who asked to be brought home, the fleet met a storm on the way, the ships were wrecked, and only a small number were saved. The de Franceschi were among the survivors, and at Venice were admitted to the *veneta cittadinanza originaria*.

cards.line: The Dalmatian line — Omiš and Imotski
cards.why: A soldier paid off in ruined land
cards.text: **Zuane Ivan Franceschi** and his brothers Frane and Matija raised a company of 250 men in July 1717 and carried the cost themselves; the pay ran two months late and was halved to ten soldi a day and a piece of ship's biscuit. Zuane took Imotski before the main Venetian army arrived and was the first man through the outer wall, where he raised the flag of St Mark. General Emo, reporting to Venice on 1 August 1717: «našao sam zauzet Varoš zaslugom Zuane Franceschija» — I found the town already taken, by the merit of Zuane Franceschi. It is in the dispatch, not in family tradition. Venice paid him in the *begluk* of the arci-beg Čaušević on the Vrljika — a house, a Turkish tower and eight mills — and it was wrecked. He went bankrupt on the campaign. Of the seventy Venetians living at Imotski after 1717, only this family settled permanently.

cards.arms: A Greek cross, two arrows and a pomegranate
cards.text: **This is the family this archive descends from, and it is the only one of the three that arrived on foot, for work.** The surname is in the Moncalvo di Pisino baptism book from 1661, and in November 1686 a **Gian Battista** died there, called in the parish document *il vecchio stipite del ramo dei De Franceschi* — the old stock of the branch. In 1711 his descendant cut ANNO · DOMNI · 1711 over a door at Gologorica; Carlo De Franceschi, writing in the 1870s, named the builder as his great-great-great-grandfather «Giambattista del fu Leonardo». Behind that lies **Mione**, in the Val di Gorto above Ovaro, where a Zuane De Franceschi appears on the 1679 headmen's list working in the Habsburg County of Pazin — the very county the Istrian villages sit in. Dean Brhan puts the family «presente in Istria dal 1650 circa, originaria di Mione». What they did there is on every register page: farmers, then masons. Joannes Baptista born 1787, *agricola*. Antonius born 1825, *lapidarius*. Josephus born 1863, stonecutter and then factory hand.

rows.lab: The strongest single fact for Crete is not the shipwreck
rows.text: The flight of 1669 is carried in every compilation and documented in none of them — Puhmajer's only authority for it is an encyclopaedia of 2001. Two other things are much harder. In **1674 the Republic assigned Zorzi de Franceschi a pension** for his services in the War of Candia; after the Turkish conquest he went from Candia to Zante and from Zante to Sebenico, and a document of **1730 directs that the pension be drawn at Capodistria «probabilmente perchè la famiglia viveva già a Seghetto»**. The French suspended it and the Austrians restored it. That is a hundred and fifty years of a Venetian war pension following one family from Crete to Istria. And **Marc'Antonio de Franceschi (1671–1758)**, the physician who bought the Seget estate in 1720, married in 1727 «Crissulla Marulli» — Chrysoula Marulli, a Cretan noble surname — and had eleven children by her. Puhmajer names her and moves straight on. She is the best evidence in his whole book for where these people came from.

rows.lab: Perinuša is not a Franceschi name
rows.text: This archive had this wrong and corrects it here. The mills on the Vrljika are not named for a Franceschi called Perin. They are named for the **Perinović** — Perin — a Zadar family the Franceschi brought in at the start of the eighteenth century as estate managers, and who followed them to their other properties. The by-name attached itself to the place and then to the owners, so that Andrija Kačić Miošić, in the *Razgovor ugodni naroda slovinskoga* of 1756, sings of the taking of Imotski and calls the commander **«Perinović Ive»**. A Venetian officer walked into Croatian epic verse under his steward's surname. A Venetian cadastral sheet of 1777 draws the stone bridge and the «Molinari di Franceschi» with eleven grindstones; fourteen were built in the end, and they ran until the end of the twentieth century.

rows.lab: How the three got confused, and how they were separated again
rows.text: By nobiliary compilation, mostly. A single surname with a Venetian count in it attracts everything else of that surname within a hundred miles. The most recent version of the error is online: a MyHeritage tree of 8,286 people descends the Crikvenica household from Zuane of Imotski, and it has been copied outward through Geni and Smart Matching since 2017. It is a magnificent pedigree and it is not ours. What separates the three is not argument but trade and register. **The Klenovica baptism of 1890 names this family's place of settlement as «Gallignana u Istriji»** — Gračišće in Istria — four generations downstream of the Gologorica house. The 1863 Gračišće entry gives the father as *lapicida*. The 1906 Crikvenica entry gives the son as «vešti klesar sada tvorničar», a skilled stonemason now a factory worker. Stonemasons coming down off an Istrian hill are not Venetian landowners on the Vrljika, and they are not Cretan counts.

The clinching detail is not in a document at all — it is on two walls. **The Seget house and the Seget tomb both carry a lion. The Gologorica house and the Gologorica tomb carry a Greek cross with two arrows and a pomegranate.** The *Blasonario Giuliano* lists four separate families of this surname in the region: one with a stork on a mount of three peaks, one with a lion, one with Carlo's cross and arrows and pomegranate, and one at Pisino with a half-castle. And **Carlo De Franceschi himself**, of the Gologorica house, writing in 1879 about the owners of Seget, called them «la nobile famiglia De Franceschi, attuale posseditrice, **emigrata dall'isola di Candia**» — the noble De Franceschi family, the present owner, emigrated from the island of Candia. Our own ancestor, describing them, described them as somebody else. **One qualification, added September 2026.** The Dalmatian family bears a lion too — Heyer von Rosenfeld draws the Franceschi shield party per fess, a lion rampant within it and a second lion issuing from the crown above, azure over or. So of the three arrivals, two bear lions and one does not, and the one that does not is the one this archive descends from. That is not an argument that Seget and Omiš are the same house; a lion in that posture is one of the commonest charges there is. It is a reason not to lean on the arms alone.

rows.lab: What would join them, and has not
rows.text: Nothing here proves the three are unrelated at some depth — a Franceschi is a son of Francesco, and the name was made independently wherever Italian was spoken. What is claimed is narrower and firmer: **no document in this archive joins any two of them**, and the people best placed to make the join declined to. Kobler had the Fiume civic registers and Carlo's own letters in front of him, and refused to unite even the three Fiume stocks he had found. The Seget family's own 1896 descent chart has not been read; the Imotski family's Zadar and Omiš papers have been read by a local historian and produce no Istrian link. Until one of those turns up a name in common, three arrivals is what the evidence supports, and three is what this site publishes.

rows.lab: The Carnians were one of the recognised peoples of Istria — and the description fits this family exactly
rows.text:
Darko Darovec's survey of early-modern migration into Istria opens with Prospero Petronio, writing in **1681** from the bishop of Novigrad's notes of forty years earlier, listing the *gente* then living in the province. The second of them: «**The Carni — many called them Cargnelli or Karnjeli** — were related to the Friulians, who were their neighbours.» They spun wool and wove cloth and linen, and worked as **tailors, smiths, shoemakers and stonemasons**. They were reasonable and frugal, «so that many soon at least recovered materially, if they did not get rich as well». Their qualities were very useful to the province. **They lived in fortified villages — *castelli* — and in the small towns**, and they had not arrived before the Slavs.

That is not a description of a peculiar family. It is a description of a **class of immigrant**, written down by a contemporary, and the Gologorica house sits inside it without adjustment: Carnian, artisan and small-owner, in a *castello*, comfortable enough within three generations to raise a small palace with an arcaded portico and a shield on the façade.

rows.lab: And the towns he names are our towns
rows.text: Darovec is precise about where the Friulian-Carnian stratum settled on the Austrian side: «a stratum of Italian and Friulian-Carnian origin had established itself in the small towns and other settlements of Austrian or Inner Istria, **particularly in Pazin, Pićan, Gradišće, Žminj and Tinjan**.» Gologorica lies between Pićan and Gračišće, in the County of Pazin, and Gračišće is the parish this line's registers are in. **Every place in his list is within fifteen kilometres of the house.** The Carnian arrival about 1700 stops being a family story and becomes a late instance of a documented movement.

rows.lab: The mechanism that turned Defranceschi into Defrančeski, named in the literature
rows.text:
The same page carries the thing the Name page has been arguing from surname evidence alone: «the immigrant Friulians and Carnians were **eventually Slavicised or Croatised** (for example, *Callegarich*, *Furlanich*) in the countryside and the Slavs Italianised (for example, *Ivich*, *Bellasich*, *Slocovich*) in the towns». Cossar, writing in 1930, found that Friulians «assimilated **surprisingly swiftly**» among the local population.

*Furlanich* is literally *the Friulian* with a Slavic patronymic ending. So the change this archive tracks — De Franceschi to Defranceschi to **Defrančeski** — is the standard Istrian outcome for exactly this kind of family, in exactly this country, and not a peculiarity of ours.

rows.lab: The Cretan arrival had a state programme behind it, and it ended in 1669
rows.text: The Seget tradition says a family came out of Crete when Candia fell. Darovec supplies what the tradition never does — the machinery. Venice attempted **twelve organised settlements of some 4,000 Greeks from Nafplio, Monemvasia, Crete and Cyprus into Istria between 1530 and 1669**. They were ineffective: harsh conditions and conflict with the locals sent many home or elsewhere. But of those who stayed, «**those that remained integrated into the predominant Italian population, since they were mostly settled in urban areas**». Two things follow. **The terminal date of the whole programme is 1669** — the year Candia surrendered, and the year the Seget tradition names. And the outcome Darovec describes — settled in a town, absorbed into the Italian-speaking population, leaving no Greek trace behind — is exactly what the Umag family looks like: an Italian-speaking house at a coastal town, with one Cretan surname surviving in it, **Crissulla Marulli**, married in 1727. Inferred The paper does not name this family. What it does is move the Crete story from *unlikely* to *the ordinary case*.

rows.lab: A footnote for the Corsican lane
rows.text: In November 1600 the captain of Rašpor, Francesco Correr, counted his garrison by nationality: **330 Italians, 48 Frenchmen, 106 Croatians and 90 Corsicans**. So there were Corsicans in Istria, in numbers, three generations before either of our arrivals — as paid soldiers. It changes nothing about the Corsican line, which this archive has closed as unconnected. It is here because it is the kind of fact that would otherwise be used, one day, to connect them.

source_arr: Seget: Damir Puhmajer's monograph on the Seget estate, read with the *voce* of the Istrian encyclopaedia and the 1903 volume of the *Atti e memorie della Società istriana*; the field photographs of the Umag tomb and the Seget house, 2026. Imotski: Vesna Kljajić-Grbavac (attrib.), «Obitelj de Franceschi u Imotskom od 1717. do danas», built on Ante Ujević's *Imotska krajina*, fra Karlo Jurišić's thesis of 1972 and the Zadar and Omiš archives. Gologorica: Carlo De Franceschi's letters to Kobler, the Moncalvo and Gračišće registers, the 1679 headmen's list of the County of Pazin, and Dean Brhan's papers in the *Atti* of the Rovigno centre. Arms: the *Blasonario Giuliano* and the family's own field photographs. Migration context: Darko Darovec, «Migration to Istria and the North Adriatic in the Modern Age: society, culture and environment», in Flocel Sabaté (ed.), *Mediterranean Towns: Mobility and Displacement of People*, Publicacions de la Presidència, Sèrie Major 10 (Barcelona: Institut d'Estudis Catalans, 2021), pp. 205–228 — read in full from the publisher's own open PDF.
